title: Graphical Rigidity of Continuous Variable Graph States under Gaussian Local Transformations
abstract: Multimode entangled pure Gaussian states are an essential resource for continuous variable (CV) quantum information processing. Menicucci et al. [2011] have shown how to describe them as graphs with complex adjacency matrices. Among such complex graph states (CGSs), quantum optics experimental setups straightforwardly display correlations described by purely imaginary graph states (iRGSs) whereas theoretical literature favors off-diagonal real graph state (RGS) descriptions, which actually reflect the entanglement structure in the infinite squeezing limit [Gonzalez-Arciniegas et al. 2021]. We study them beyond this ideal case, thus establishing in the finite squeezing regime an equivalence criterion for the generic case of CGSs through a graph propagating set of conditions which either finds a Gaussian Local Unitary (GLU) converting one state to another or gives a proof of impossibility if such a GLU does not exist. In the experimentally relevant case of the conversion between iRGSs and RGSs, the set of conditions results in simple relations between the topologies of the equivalent real and imaginary graphs. Finally, we show that the canonical forms of iRGSs and RGSs imply that the topology of the CV real and imaginary graph states are too rigid to admit any exact qumode local-addition analogue to the qubit complementation or qudit local-addition, thus demonstrating the non-existence of any exact qumode local-addition for these states. We however define an approximate one when the squeezing is strong enough.
summary: This theoretical paper investigates the structural rigidity of continuous variable graph states (CGSs) under local Gaussian transformations. It develops a set of necessary conditions to determine if one state can be transformed into another, particularly comparing imaginary and real graph states. The key finding is that these graph states are highly rigid, precluding exact local additions analogous to those in qubit systems.
main_problem: The paper establishes an equivalence criterion for generic Complex Graph States (CGSs) under Gaussian Local Unitary (GLU) transformations, focusing on the conversion between purely imaginary (iRGSs) and real (RGSs) graph states.
main_result: The topologies of iRGSs and RGSs are shown to be too rigid to admit any exact qumode local-addition analogue, though an approximate version exists in the strongly squeezed regime.
method: The analysis uses the symplectic formalism to derive a 'graph propagating set of conditions' that must be satisfied for two CGSs to be convertible via a GLU.
model_or_system: The system involves multimode entangled pure Gaussian states, mathematically described by complex adjacency matrices (CGSs), which include the purely imaginary (iRGSs) and real (RGSs) variants.
key_observables: The matrices $\sigma_{jk}$ (derived from the adjacency matrix $Z$), whose rank and determinant are used as GLU-invariants.
important_parameters: The squeezing parameter ($\lambda$), the finite squeezing regime (moving beyond the infinite limit), and the structure of the local transformations.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the states are pure Gaussian states with vanishing first moments, and the final approximate results rely on strong squeezing limits.
figures_summary: The notes mention a Table D.1 summarizing the rank of $\sigma_{jk}$ matrices for RGSs and iRGSs, and various equations detailing transformation relationships between matrices $F$ and $H$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the mathematical framework using symplectic formalism, deriving necessary GLU-invariants ($\sigma_{jk}$), establishing the equivalence criteria for different state types (CGS, iRGS, RGS), and finally analyzing the implications for local operations, including the approximate local addition.
why_interesting: This work provides deep structural constraints on entanglement resources (Gaussian states) used in quantum computation, showing fundamental limitations on local operations that are crucial for designing robust quantum protocols.
